mission.title: Media Literacy, Source Evaluation and Information Integrity

theory.title: Media Literacy, Source Evaluation and Information Integrity
theory.explanation: This mission develops advanced media literacy. Effective C2 communication requires writers and speakers to make purpose, audience, evidence and degree of certainty explicit. Analyse the context before choosing a register; distinguish established information from interpretation; organise complex material so that decisions and qualifications remain visible.
theory.tip: Use precise terminology, attribute claims, qualify uncertainty and make the requested action explicit.

patterns.label: Define purpose and audience
patterns.pattern: Identify what the audience needs to know or decide.
examples: State the decision required before presenting supporting detail.

patterns.label: Support and qualify
patterns.pattern: Connect each claim to evidence and state relevant limitations.
examples: The findings suggest a pattern, although the sample is not representative.

patterns.label: Structure for action
patterns.pattern: Use signposting, headings and explicit ownership.
examples: The recommendation is assigned to a named lead for review by an agreed date.

patterns.label: Review for integrity
patterns.pattern: Check terminology, attribution, tone and consistency.
examples: Distinguish verified outcomes from projected benefits.

content.passage:
A short video showing a public official making a controversial statement spread rapidly across several platforms. The clip appeared to be clear evidence, but the original upload contained no date, location or link to the full recording. A local journalist traced the footage to a longer event published months earlier. The sentence in the viral clip had been preceded by a qualification that changed its meaning.

The journalist compared the full recording with the event transcript and contacted two people who had attended. The sources corroborated the date and setting, although one transcript contained a minor transcription error. The final article embedded the complete recording, described the verification process and distinguished what could be established from what remained uncertain.

The case illustrates why provenance and context matter. A clip can be authentic and still mislead when it is selectively edited. The journalist did not claim to know who had removed the qualification or why. Instead, the article documented the source trail and avoided attributing intent without evidence. Information integrity depended on transparent method as much as on the final conclusion.
